tagline: Container images built fast, kept small and shipped without known vulnerabilities.
overview: Docker problems are usually build problems in disguise. We rewrite Dockerfiles around multi-stage builds and layer ordering so a change to application code reuses the expensive dependency layers instead of rebuilding the world every time. Builds move to a shared cache and a repeatable base image, which keeps laptops and CI producing the same thing.

The other half is what ends up in the image. We strip build toolchains and package managers from the runtime layer, run as a non-root user, pin digests where supply-chain risk matters, and produce a software bill of materials for each release. Images that were once a gigabyte routinely come down by more than half, which speeds up every pull and narrows the patching surface.
problems: A one-line change triggers a fifteen-minute image rebuild
Images carry compilers, package managers and root users into production
It works on a laptop and fails in the pipeline
Nobody can say what packages are inside a running image

includes.title: Dockerfile redesign
includes.text: Layer ordering, multi-stage targets and cache mounts arranged so the slow steps sit at the bottom and rebuild only when their inputs change.

includes.title: Image slimming
includes.text: Runtime layers built from distroless or Alpine bases with build tooling removed, dropping image size and the number of packages you have to patch later.

includes.title: Hardened runtime defaults
includes.text: Non-root users, read-only root filesystems and dropped Linux capabilities, with a documented exception path when a workload genuinely needs to run as root.

includes.title: Registry and tagging
includes.text: A tag convention that maps every image back to a commit, immutable digests for production, and retention rules so the registry does not fill with untagged layers.

includes.title: Local development parity
includes.text: Compose files and dev containers that mirror the deployed image closely enough that environment differences stop being the first suspect in every bug report.

includes.title: Build verification
includes.text: Scans for base-image CVEs, secrets and licence issues wired into the build, so a bad image is caught before it reaches a registry production can pull from.

deliverables: Rewritten Dockerfiles with documented layer strategy
Shared cache configuration for local and CI builds
Image size and vulnerability baseline report
Tagging, retention and registry policy document
Local compose setup matching the deployed image

process.title: Audit the build images
process.text: We time a cold and a warm build, trace where the layers come from, and check what the runtime image actually contains before changing anything.

process.title: Rebuild for caching
process.text: Dockerfiles are restructured so dependency layers change rarely and code layers change often, with cache mounts for package managers that support them.

process.title: Harden the runtime
process.text: We switch to minimal bases, remove build tooling, add a non-root user and fix whatever breaks, which is usually a file permission or a missing shell.

process.title: Wire it into the pipeline
process.text: Scans, digests and retention run on every build, and we hand over the Dockerfile conventions so new services start from a good image.

faqs.q: Will slimming images break our application?
faqs.a: Occasionally, yes — normally when something relied on a shell, a package manager or a library that was present by accident. We stage the change, run the test suite against the new image and add anything genuinely required rather than abandoning the approach.

faqs.q: Do we need to move off our current base image?
faqs.a: Not always. If a maintained base already gives you a small runtime and timely security updates, the gains from switching are modest. The bigger wins usually come from layer ordering, cache use and what you copy into the final stage.

faqs.q: How does this relate to our Kubernetes setup?
faqs.a: Better images make the cluster easier to run: faster pulls, smaller nodes, fewer CVEs to patch and less chance of a container needing privileged access. The two pieces of work reinforce each other, but the image changes stand alone if you are not on Kubernetes yet.

faqs.q: Can you work with our existing Dockerfiles?
faqs.a: Yes, and that is the usual starting point. Most Dockerfiles have a sound shape and two or three expensive mistakes. We keep the structure, fix the ordering and caching, and rewrite only the stages that are clearly working against you.

seo.title: Docker & Containerization — Fast, Small, Secure Images
seo.description: Rebuilt Dockerfiles with multi-stage caching, slimmer runtime images and build-time scanning, so containers are fast to pull and easier to patch.
